abstract: BACKGROUND: Crop losses caused by insect pests are expected to increase under global warming, highlighting the need for accurate phenology forecasts to support integrated pest management (IPM). Arthropod pests, as ectotherms, exhibit temperature-dependent development and phenology that can be described by thermal performance curves (TPCs). For decades, developmental models have predicted pest emergence through thermal accumulation approaches, yet it remains unclear to what extent experimentally derived development models can accurately predict field phenology across spatial and temporal scales. Here, we evaluate whether developmental TPCs and linear degree-day models fitted from published experimental data can predict large-scale pest phenology under a rate-summation approach. RESULTS: We compiled published developmental data for the widespread crucifer pest Pieris rapae and fitted several TPCs and linear degree-day models. Model predictions were validated against independent long-term monitoring data from the Catalan Butterfly Monitoring Scheme for mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands. Published experimental data accurately predicted large-scale pest emergence, with prediction errors generally below one week. However, predictive performance depended strongly on the spatial and temporal scale considered, with model rankings changing according to the scale and temperature resolution used. CONCLUSION: Published experimental thermal biology data can accurately predict regional insect pest phenology when developmental models are selected according to the intended forecasting scale. These findings provide practical guidance for improving pest alert systems and other decision-support tools, while demonstrating how decades of experimental research can be translated into operational phenology forecasting.
